Fermion. Fermions are particles with half-integer spin—one-half, three-halves, five-halves—that obey Fermi-Dirac statistics, including the Pauli exclusion principle. The Standard Model's matter consists of leptons and quarks, both fundamental fermions, while baryons are composite fermionic hadrons. Fermions are the building blocks of matter and distinctly contrast with integer-spin bosons.

Half-integer spin particles are fundamentally different from bosons. Fermions obey Fermi-Dirac statistics, which means they are antisymmetric under particle exchange. Most importantly, they are subject to the Pauli exclusion principle: no two identical fermions can occupy the same quantum state. The Standard Model contains six leptons—the electron, muon, tau, and their corresponding neutrinos—and six quarks spanning up, down, charm, strange, bottom, and top. Baryons like protons and neutrons are composite fermions made of three quarks. Every fermion has a corresponding antimatter partner.

The division between fermions and bosons is among the deepest symmetries in physics, with profound consequences for the structure of matter. The electron's fermionic nature explains chemical periodicity and atomic stability. When non-relativistic fermions accumulate, they resist compression through quantum pressure, a phenomenon that prevents stellar collapse and shapes the universe's end states. Electrons in white dwarfs and neutrons in neutron stars survive through this degeneracy pressure, all rooted in the fermionic nature of these particles.
